name: Maghull North station
text: Maghull North station, at one end of this stretch, is one of Merseyrail's newest: it opened on June 18th 2018 to serve the north end of Maghull, on the Northern Line.

name: Switch Island
text: Your train passes near Switch Island, on the train's {side}, the junction where the M57 and M58 motorways both end and meet the A59. It carries up to 100,000 vehicles a day and has been called one of England's busiest motorway junctions.

name: Rampworx skatepark
text: Your train passes near Rampworx, on the train's {side}, an indoor skatepark for skateboarders, BMX riders, rollerbladers and scooter riders. It is the largest indoor skatepark in the United Kingdom.

name: Aintree Institute
text: Your train passes near the site of the Aintree Institute, on the train's {side}, a hall where the Beatles played 31 shows between January 1961 and January 1962, billed as "The Dynamic Beatles". It was pulled down in 2007.

name: HM Prison Liverpool
text: Your train passes near HM Prison Liverpool, on the train's {side}, long known as Walton Gaol. It was built between 1848 and 1855 to replace an older gaol in the centre of Liverpool that had grown too small.

name: St Mary's Church, Walton
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Walton, on the train's {side}, once the parish church for the area that became the city of Liverpool. A church here is mentioned in the Domesday Book; the present one was rebuilt after bombs destroyed most of it, all but the 1830s tower, in the May Blitz of 1941.

name: Bootle War Memorial
text: Your train passes near Bootle War Memorial, on the train's {side}, in King's Gardens on Stanley Road. Herman Cawthra's monument has a mother and child on top of an obelisk, surrounded by three servicemen; it was unveiled in 1922 and is listed Grade II*.

name: Bootle Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Bootle Town Hall, on the train's {side}, opened in 1882 in the Renaissance style with a two-stage clock tower. It is now the headquarters of Sefton Council.

name: Seaforth House
text: Your train passes near the site of Seaforth House, on the train's {side}, a mansion built in 1813 for Sir John Gladstone, father of the Prime Minister William Ewart Gladstone. Gladstone named Seaforth himself, after the title of Lord Seaforth, head of his second wife's mother's family.

name: Old Christ Church, Waterloo
text: Your train passes near Old Christ Church, Waterloo, on the train's {side}, built in the 1890s by the Lancaster firm of Paley, Austin and Paley from red sandstone quarried in Bootle. The Buildings of England calls it one of the firm's "very finest" churches; it is now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

name: Crosby Beach
text: Your train passes near Crosby Beach, on the train's {side}, permanent home since 2007 of Antony Gormley's Another Place sculptures. Gormley chose it because he thought the beach "the opposite of pretty": "terrific and brutal", a working beach.

name: Waterloo Rugby Club
text: Your train passes Waterloo Rugby Club's ground, on the train's {side}, home since 1892 of a club founded in 1882 and once a power in English rugby union. Will Greenwood, Kyran Bracken and Austin Healey have played for it.

name: Crosby Battery
text: Your train passes near the site of Crosby Battery, on the train's {side}, built in the sand dunes in 1906 and 1907 to guard the mouth of the River Mersey. In the Second World War its guns defended the port against ships and aircraft.

name: Altcar Training Camp
text: Your train passes Altcar Training Camp, on the train's {side}, a firing range of beaches, marshland and woods. The 4th Earl of Sefton first lent the land for the Grand Lancashire Rifle Contest in 1860 and gave it to the Volunteer Forces two years later.

name: Formby Golf Club
text: Your train passes near Formby Golf Club, on the train's {side}, a links course founded in 1884 and redesigned by Willie Park Jr in 1912. It hosted the Curtis Cup in 2004 and the Amateur Championship four times.

name: RAF Woodvale
text: Your train passes near RAF Woodvale, on the train's {side}, built as a night fighter airfield to defend Liverpool. It opened in December 1941, just after the Liverpool Blitz, and Polish Spitfire squadrons were among the first to fly from it.

name: Royal Birkdale Golf Club
text: Your train passes near Royal Birkdale Golf Club, on the train's {side}, which has hosted the Open Championship 11 times between 1954 and 2026. Arnold Palmer, Tom Watson and Jordan Spieth are among its Open winners, and it hosted the Ryder Cup in 1965 and 1969.

name: Trafalgar Road Ground
text: Your train passes the Trafalgar Road Ground, on the train's {side}, home of Southport & Birkdale Cricket Club. It has hosted first-class county cricket since 1959, when Lancashire played Worcestershire here.

name: British Lawnmower Museum
text: Your train passes near the British Lawnmower Museum, on the train's {side}, with more than 300 restored machines from the last 200 years. Among them are mowers once owned by Prince Charles and Princess Diana, Brian May and Paul O'Grady.

name: The Atkinson
text: Your train passes near the Atkinson, on the train's {side}, Southport's art gallery and library on Lord Street. It was paid for by William Atkinson, a cotton manufacturer from Knaresborough who often visited the town, and opened in 1878.

name: Southport gas holder
text: Your train passes near the site of the Southport gas holder, on the train's {side}. Built in 1969 and 84.5 metres high, it was the tallest structure in Southport for 40 years and could be seen from Blackpool and Winter Hill, until it was taken down.

name: New Lane station
text: New Lane station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1855 and keeps its stone station building, now a private house. The Martin Mere bird sanctuary is about a mile's walk away.

name: St John the Baptist Church, Burscough
text: Your train passes near St John the Baptist Church, Burscough, on the train's {side}, built between 1829 and 1832 with a grant from the Church Building Commission. It is listed Grade II*.

name: Burscough Curves
text: Your train passes the site of the Burscough Curves, short links that once let trains run between this line and the Ormskirk to Preston line. The north curve was cut in 1969 and the south curve saw its last train in 1982.

name: Our Lady and All Saints Church, Parbold
text: Your train passes near Our Lady and All Saints Church, Parbold, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church built between 1878 and 1884 and paid for by the Ainscough family, whose firm sold flour. Its architect was Edmund Kirby.

name: Appley Bridge meteorite
text: Your train passes near where the Appley Bridge meteorite landed, on the train's {side}: it hit a field at Halliwell Farm at about 8.45pm on October 13th 1914 and was found the next day, looking like burnt iron.

name: Gathurst Viaduct
text: Your train passes under Gathurst Viaduct, which carries the M6 motorway across the Douglas valley, over the railway, the Leeds and Liverpool Canal and the River Douglas. Built in 1961, it is the second largest bridge on the M6.

name: Wigan Pier
text: Your train passes near Wigan Pier, on the train's {side}, beside the Leeds and Liverpool Canal. One story of the name dates from 1891, when a Southport excursion train stopped near here by a long wooden gantry and a passenger was jokingly told it was Wigan's "pier".

name: All Saints' Church, Wigan
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, on the train's {side}, Wigan's parish church on a hill in the centre of the town. The lower parts of its tower date from the late 13th century; the rest was rebuilt between 1845 and 1850 by Sharpe and Paley.

name: St Matthew's Church, Highfield
text: Your train passes near St Matthew's Church, Highfield, on the train's {side}, built between 1892 and 1894 and paid for by Colonel Henry Blundell-Hollinshead-Blundell, owner of the Pemberton Colliery, in memory of his wife Beatrice. It is listed Grade II*.

name: St Luke's Church, Orrell
text: Your train passes near St Luke's Church, Orrell, on the train's {side}, designed by Henry Paley of Austin and Paley. Building began in 1926, but it was not finished until 1939, and the planned tower was never built.

name: Rainford station
text: Rainford station, at one end of this stretch, was built in 1858 as Rainford Junction, where the line met branches to Skelmersdale and St Helens. Both branches lost their passenger trains in the 1950s.

name: Headbolt Lane station
text: Headbolt Lane station, at one end of this stretch, opened on October 5th 2023, where Merseyrail's electric Northern Line meets the line to Wigan. A station here had been wanted since 1972.

name: St Chad's Church, Kirkby
text: Your train passes near St Chad's Church, Kirkby, on the train's {side}, on a site with a church in the Domesday Book. The present red sandstone church, by Paley and Austin, was built between 1869 and 1871 and paid for by the 4th Earl of Sefton, with stone from his own quarries.

name: Valentine's Brook
text: Your train passes near Valentine's Brook, on the train's {side}, a fence on Aintree's Grand National course, jumped twice in the race. It is named after a horse called Valentine, said to have jumped it hind legs first in 1840.

name: Walton Centre
text: Your train passes near the Walton Centre, on the train's {side}, a specialist hospital for neurology and neurosurgery. Its wards are named after pioneering neurosurgeons, and it moved here in 1998 from Walton Hospital on Rice Lane.

name: Devonfield Garden
text: Your train passes near Devonfield Garden, on the train's {side}, a park in north Liverpool. In 2010 it was one of 17 parks in the city to win a Green Flag Award.

name: Swan and Railway Hotel
text: Your train passes the Swan and Railway Hotel, on the train's {side}, a pub built in 1898 beside the bridge that carries the West Coast Main Line over Wallgate. The Campaign for Real Ale rates its interior as being of special national historic importance.

name: Coppull Mill
text: Your train passes Coppull Mill, on the train's {side}, a cotton spinning mill opened in 1906; with its sister Mavis Mill it employed 700 people. Its 1,600 horsepower engine drove the mill through 36 ropes, and the building is now an enterprise centre.

name: British Commercial Vehicle Museum
text: Your train passes near the British Commercial Vehicle Museum, on the train's {side}, on part of the old Leyland Motors factory site. Its buses and early fire engines include the armour-plated Popemobile British Leyland built for the Pope's visit in 1982.
